title: Post-fire regeneration increases plant quality and insect herbivore performance
content:
Abstract
The frequency and extent of wildfire are increasing across the Western United States, with far-reaching ecological impacts. Herbivorous insects are among the first organisms to recolonize post-burn landscapes; however, the factors that shape insect performance on plants after fire are poorly understood. In many fire-adapted ecosystems, woody plants resprout from their root crown, representing some of the first plant tissue available. This resprouting plant tissue may vary in nutritional and defensive traits, with implications for insect herbivores: if leaves are higher-quality after fire, this could improve survival and growth, increasing rates of ecological reassembly. In contrast, lower-quality tissue could impede reestablishment of these critical interactions at the base of the food web. Here, we measure plant traits and insect herbivore performance on resprouting plant tissue after fire. We use a native shrub, rubber rabbitbrush (Ericameria nauseosa: Asteraceae) Pall. ex Pursh (G.L. Nesom & G.I. Baird), a common member of fire-prone, semi-arid ecosystems in the West, and leverage a recent wildfire in Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument, Utah. To measure herbivore performance, we conducted a bioassay with caterpillars of a native generalist butterfly, the painted lady (Vanessa cardui) (Linnaeus, 1758) (Lepidoptera: Nymphalidae). We also measured plant biomass (plant and leaf size) and 2 leaf nutritional traits (specific leaf area; water content). We found that caterpillars had higher survival and growth on resprouting plant tissue. Rabbitbrush leaves were also larger and higher in water content. These results suggest that food web reassembly after fire may be facilitated by shifts in plant traits.
